hints.junior: The agent retried a failing tool call sixty-some times over twenty minutes — nobody saw a number climbing, the invoice was the first signal.
hints.mid: Each retry re-sent the growing failure history, so every retry cost more than the last — a compounding loop, not a flat one.
hints.staff: Every other metered resource gets a visible running total somewhere — token spend on an agent loop usually doesn't, because it was built as a chat feature, not a budgeted resource.

hints.junior: Click Simulate session in each mode and watch what each one shows you — and whether it ever stops on its own.
hints.mid: Same retry loop both times — the difference is a visible meter, a model downgrade at the warning line, and a hard stop at the cap.
hints.staff: Per-retry cost climbs in both modes — that's the re-sent context. The fixed mode doesn't slow that growth, it bounds and surfaces it.

hints.junior: Count tokens live, show the running total in the UI, and set a hard per-session cap that does something automatically when it's hit.
hints.mid: Graceful degradation means a cheaper model at a warning threshold and blocked calls at the hard cap — not a silent overrun, not a raw error.
hints.staff: Scope the cap per session, not a global daily total — a global cap just delays the same failure and then blocks everyone at once instead of containing one runaway conversation.

hints.junior: The meter has to update between individual tool calls, not just full agent turns — a loop that never finishes a turn never updates a turn-scoped counter.
hints.mid: Decide what 'graceful' means — downgrade vs. hard block — before an incident forces you to improvise the answer live.
hints.staff: Enforce the cap server-side — a UI meter that stops updating is a display bug, not a spend control, if the backend keeps processing calls regardless.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about a support agent that retried a broken tool call over and over, for twenty minutes, with absolutely no cost signal visible anywhere.
sections.mid: Every retry re-sent the conversation so far, including previous failed attempts and their errors, so each retry's cost was larger than the last with no cost signal visible anywhere.
sections.staff: This isn't a model-cost problem, it's a missing-feedback-loop problem — every other metered resource in a product gets a visible running total, but token spend on an agent loop usually doesn't.

sections.junior: The fix is three things: track cost per session as it happens, show that number somewhere in the UI, and set a hard cap that does something automatic once it's hit, instead of just running forever.
sections.mid: At a warning threshold, switch to a cheaper model for the rest of the conversation; at the hard cap, stop making tool calls and tell the user, rather than a silent continue or a raw crash.
sections.staff: Scope the budget to a session, not a global daily total — a global cap just delays the same failure and blocks every user at once, while a per-session cap contains a single runaway loop.

sections.junior: Run the same retry loop in both modes and see the difference: one shows you nothing, the other shows a live meter, downgrades the model, and eventually stops itself.
sections.mid: The broken mode has no meter and no cap, so the loop keeps running and getting more expensive per retry. The fixed mode shows the running cost and swaps to a cheaper model at the warning threshold.
sections.staff: The per-retry cost still grows in both modes — the fixed mode doesn't stop that growth, it just makes it visible and bounded instead of invisible.

sections.junior: If an agent can retry itself, it can retry itself into a huge bill. Give it a visible running cost and a hard stop, so a bug becomes an annoyance instead of an invoice surprise.
sections.mid: Track cost per session live, surface it in the UI, and degrade gracefully — a cheaper model at the warning threshold, blocked calls at the hard cap.
sections.staff: Check the cap between individual tool calls, not full turns, and enforce it server-side — a UI meter alone is visibility, not a spend control.
